texts.0: SP, due to a leg heading flown without any drift correction after roll-out, did not maintain the planned ground track and did not correct the deviation as soon as practical. Displacement from the course line passed 2 NM and continued to increase toward the edge of the planned route corridor. The IP had to take the aircraft back toward the course line and re-establish the leg.
texts.1: SP, due to a wind correction angle applied late and in one direction only, allowed displacement from the planned ground track to reach the 2 NM limit. The return to the course line was started only after verbal prompting from the IP. The correction was slow enough that the following checkpoint was still crossed off track.
texts.2: SP, due to a shallow initial correction after rolling out on the leg heading, drifted between 1 and 2 NM from the planned ground track. SP recognized the displacement at the next visual reference, applied a positive correction angle and regained the course line before the following checkpoint. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the planned ground track within 1 NM throughout the route. Corrections were applied early, in the correct direction and with an appropriate magnitude. Each checkpoint was crossed on the planned course line.
texts.4: SP held the planned ground track with deviations that were barely measurable on the chart. Drift was anticipated ahead of each leg turn and the correction angle was set immediately on roll-out. The aircraft tracked directly over every checkpoint of the route.
texts.marginal: SP kept displacement from the planned ground track inside the standards, but the deviations were consistently near the wider tolerance and always to the downwind side. The trend indicates a drift correction that is applied after the error appears rather than anticipated. SP is expected to set the correction angle on roll-out for each leg and hold the track error inside the tighter tolerance.

texts_at.0: With the IP applying the wind correction angle for each leg and calling out the heading to hold, SP flew the assigned leg heading while beginning to compare the ground picture with the chart. Judging drift from the ground picture and sizing a wind correction angle have not yet been asked of SP, so track-keeping still depends on the IP's inputs at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin naming the drift observed on the ground, with the IP still applying the correction angle, before an independent standard is asked for.
texts_at.1: SP held the displacement from the planned ground track at about 1.8 NM, correcting back toward the course line before the next checkpoint. The residual came from a wind correction angle applied a little late after roll-out, which let the drift build before the first adjustment. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to apply the correction angle immediately on roll-out so the displacement does not approach the 2 NM limit.
texts_at.2: SP kept the displacement from the planned ground track at about 1.5 NM, correcting toward the course line as the leg progressed. The offset traced to a shallow initial wind correction angle after roll-out, which needed a second adjustment to close. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to size the first correction angle to the observed drift so a second adjustment is not required.
texts_at.3: SP held the planned ground track within about 0.8 NM throughout the route, crossing each checkpoint close to the course line. The small residual came from a wind correction angle set slightly light for the actual drift on one leg. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to cross-check the correction angle against the observed drift a little earlier on each leg to remove the remaining offset.

texts_above.1: SP flew the assigned leg heading and closed the developing displacement from the planned ground track to about 1.9 NM before the wind correction was completed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP corrected every developing displacement from the planned ground track before it passed about 1.5 NM, applying a positive wind correction angle at the first indication of drift. Making that first correction angle slightly larger would close the track even sooner on a long leg. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good track correction technique.
texts_above.3: SP held the planned ground track within about 0.8 NM on every leg, applying the wind correction angle in a single deliberate step after each roll-out. The technique is already sound; only the shortest legs still call for a touch of anticipation before the drift is visible. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good drift correction discipline.
texts_above.4: SP tracked the planned ground track with deviations inside about 0.2 NM on every leg, anticipating the drift before roll-out was complete each time. The only refinement available was to log the applied correction angle for the debrief, since the flying itself left nothing to add. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent ground track precision.

texts.0: SP, due to an absent cross-check of aircraft position against the planned course line, did not correct the track deviation as soon as practical. The error was allowed to build through most of the leg and the displacement passed 2 NM before any action was taken. The IP directed both the recognition of the error and the turn back to course.
texts.1: SP, due to a position cross-check performed only at the planned checkpoints and never between them, recognized the track deviation only after it had reached the 2 NM limit. The correction was initiated after verbal prompting from the IP. The aircraft regained the course line late in the following leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that lapsed while the chart was being handled in the cockpit, detected the track error one to two miles off the planned line. Once the scan was resumed SP identified the displacement, turned toward the course line without prompting and re-established the track before the next turning point.
texts.3: SP cross-checked position against the planned course line continuously and corrected each track deviation as soon as it appeared. Errors were caught inside one mile and removed with a single correctly sized correction.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous cross-check between the chart, the ground picture and the navigation display, so track errors were identified while they were still forming. Each correction was small, immediate and required no follow-up action.
texts.marginal: SP corrected every track deviation inside the standards, but the corrections were consistently started at the checkpoint rather than as soon as the error appeared. The trend is a cross-check driven by checkpoints instead of a continuous comparison of position with the course line. SP is expected to compare position against the planned line between checkpoints and act on the first indication of drift.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling attention back to the course line each time the cross-check lapsed, SP compared aircraft position against the planned course line at the checkpoints called out. Holding a continuous cross-check between checkpoints, rather than only at them, is a skill the Training Section has not yet asked SP to demonstrate independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to compare position against the course line at least once between checkpoints, with the IP still available to prompt the comparison.
texts_at.1: SP corrected the track deviation with the displacement at about 1.8 NM, closing back to the course line during the following leg. The delayed recognition traced to a position cross-check performed only at the checkpoints rather than between them. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to compare position against the course line at least once between checkpoints so the deviation is caught before it nears the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP corrected each track deviation with the displacement held to about 1.5 NM, regaining the course line before the next turning point. The offset came from a brief lapse in the position cross-check while the chart was being folded for the next leg. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to complete chart handling on the straight portion of the leg so the cross-check is not interrupted.
texts_at.3: SP cross-checked position against the course line continuously and held the track error to about 0.7 NM on the leg where a correction was needed. The small residual came from a cross-check interval that opened slightly during a radio call. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same cross-check interval through radio calls so no leg is flown without an active comparison.

texts_above.1: SP compared position against the planned course line and closed the resulting track deviation to about 1.85 NM before the course line was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP caught every developing track deviation at about 1.4 NM through a cross-check that ran continuously between checkpoints, not only at them. The interval between position checks would close a little further still on the longer legs. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound position cross-check.
texts_above.3: SP held the track error to about 0.7 NM by comparing position against the course line on a fixed short interval throughout each leg. The technique is already sound; only the busiest checkpoints still draw the cross-check out by a second or two. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed cross-check timing.
texts_above.4: SP identified every track error while it was still inside about 0.2 NM, with the cross-check running continuously through chart work and radio calls alike. The only refinement available was to note the exact interval used for the debrief, since the scan itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional monitoring discipline.

error_modes.label: Drift assessment and wind correction angle technique

texts.0: SP, due to a correction angle guessed rather than derived from the observed drift, applied corrections that were in the wrong direction or grossly oversized. The aircraft was flown through the course line repeatedly and the resulting excursion exceeded 2 NM. The IP had to establish the heading that held the planned ground track.
texts.1: SP, due to repeated small heading changes instead of one assessed correction angle, never stabilized on a heading that held the ground track. The oscillation about the course line reached the 2 NM limit. A usable correction angle was set only after the IP called out the drift direction.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial correction angle undersized for the actual drift, remained between 1 and 2 NM off the planned track for part of the leg. SP re-estimated the drift from the movement of a ground reference, increased the correction angle and closed back to the course line without assistance.
texts.3: SP established a correction angle that matched the observed drift and held the ground track within one mile. Heading was adjusted in single deliberate steps and the aircraft remained stable on the course line.
texts.4: SP assessed the drift from the ground picture within the first mile of each leg and set a correction angle that held the aircraft on the course line for the whole leg. Heading changes were minimal and no reconvergence to the track was necessary.
texts.marginal: SP held the ground track within the standards, but the correction angle was reached through several successive heading changes rather than one assessment. The trend is a trial-and-error technique that costs time and track accuracy on short legs. SP is expected to assess drift from the ground picture once and set the full correction angle in a single step.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling out the drift direction and the size of the correction angle to apply, SP made the heading changes needed to work the aircraft back toward the course line. Estimating drift from a single ground reference and setting the full correction in one step have not yet been introduced, so the correction angle still comes from the IP's call at this stage. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin naming the drift direction observed on the ground, with the IP still confirming the size of the correction, before an independent correction angle is asked for.
texts_at.1: SP closed the track error to the course line with the displacement at about 1.9 NM before the correction angle was set. The delay came from two small heading changes tried before the drift was properly assessed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to assess the drift from a single ground reference and set the full correction angle in one step.
texts_at.2: SP re-estimated the drift and closed the aircraft to the course line with the displacement held to about 1.4 NM. The initial correction angle had been undersized for the drift actually observed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to size the first correction angle from the ground reference rather than adjusting it in a second step.
texts_at.3: SP established a correction angle that matched the observed drift and held the ground track within about 0.6 NM for the leg concerned. The small residual came from a drift estimate taken slightly early, before the wind effect was fully established. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to delay the drift estimate a few seconds longer so the correction angle is set from a stable reading.

texts_above.1: SP set a correction angle from the observed drift and closed the displacement from the planned ground track to about 1.9 NM before the course line was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP assessed the drift from a single ground reference and set a correction angle that held the track error to about 1.3 NM for the rest of the leg. Confirming the estimate against a second reference would tighten the same correction on a shorter leg. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid drift assessment.
texts_above.3: SP matched the correction angle to the observed drift in one step and held the ground track within about 0.6 NM without any further adjustment. The technique is already sound; only a crosswind leg shorter than briefed would call for a faster first estimate. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed wind correction angle technique.
texts_above.4: SP set a correction angle from the ground picture that held the track error inside about 0.2 NM for the whole leg, with no reconvergence required. The only refinement available was to call the assessed drift out loud for the record, since the correction itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding drift assessment.

error_modes.label: Recognition of wind effect and recomputation of time and fuel

texts.0: SP, due to continued use of the briefed forecast wind after the actual drift and groundspeed had clearly changed, did not recognize the wind effect in flight and did not recalculate flight time or fuel. Leg times and fuel figures remained the planned ones while the aircraft fell progressively behind the route. The IP had to provide the revised time and fuel picture.
texts.1: SP, due to a leg timing check made only at the far end of the route, recognized the wind effect only when the accumulated delay was already large. The recalculation of flight time and fuel was carried out after the IP asked for revised figures. The corrected estimates arrived too late to be of any use for that leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a groundspeed check taken over too short a segment, first accepted a leg time that did not match the actual wind. SP repeated the check over the following segment, recognized the headwind component and recalculated the remaining leg times and the fuel required without prompting.
texts.3: SP recognized the wind effect in flight from the observed drift and groundspeed and recalculated the remaining flight time and fuel when the change required it. The revised figures were consistent with the actual progress along the route.
texts.4: SP identified the difference between the forecast and the actual wind within the first leg and immediately produced revised leg times and fuel figures for the rest of the route. The estimates were accurate and were passed clearly, so the flight plan stayed current for the whole sortie.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the wind effect and produced acceptable revised time and fuel figures, but the recalculation was done once and was not refreshed as the wind changed along the route. The trend is a single update rather than continuous management of the plan. SP is expected to re-check groundspeed on each leg and revise time and fuel whenever the observed wind differs from the planned wind.

texts_at.0: With the IP identifying the change in groundspeed and providing the revised leg times and fuel figures, SP read back the updated numbers and entered them on the log. Checking groundspeed against the forecast wind and recalculating time and fuel independently have not yet been asked of SP, so the revised picture still comes from the IP at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin comparing the observed groundspeed with the forecast figure on each leg, with the IP still producing the revised time and fuel picture, before an independent recalculation is required.
texts_at.1: SP recalculated the flight time and fuel once the wind effect could no longer be ignored, producing the revised figures on the second leg of the route rather than the first. The late recognition came from a groundspeed check that was not repeated soon enough after the initial one. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to repeat the groundspeed check on every leg so a changing wind is caught before a second leg goes by unrecalculated.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the wind effect after one leg flown on the forecast figures and recalculated the remaining leg times and fuel before the next checkpoint. The delay traced to a groundspeed check taken over a shorter segment than needed to reveal the trend clearly. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to extend the first groundspeed check over a longer segment of the leg so the trend is unambiguous the first time it is checked.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the wind effect from the observed drift and groundspeed within the first leg and recalculated the remaining flight time and fuel before it was needed. The figures needed a small refinement once, when the wind continued to build through the second leg. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to refresh the recalculation again whenever the wind trend continues to change after the first update.

texts_above.1: SP recalculated the flight time and fuel once the change in wind could no longer be ignored, and closed the resulting displacement from the planned ground track to about 1.9 NM as the revised figures were applied. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the wind effect from the very first leg and recalculated flight time and fuel for the remaining route before the following checkpoint, without waiting for a second confirming check. Passing the revised ETA to the log at the same moment would leave nothing further to remember later in the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady recognition of wind effect.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the changing wind within the first few minutes of the route and kept the flight time and fuel figures current at every leg thereafter, refreshing them each time the observed drift moved. The technique is already sound; only a very short first leg would leave less time than usual to confirm the initial trend. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate time and fuel management.
texts_above.4: SP identified the difference between the forecast and the actual wind before the first checkpoint and produced accurate revised leg times and fuel figures for the whole of the remaining route in a single update. The only refinement available was to log the exact moment of the update for the debrief, since the figures themselves needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary recognition of wind effect.

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft position relative to the planned course line, lost orientation between checkpoints and continued on a heading that no longer led to the next turning point. The displacement grew past 2 NM without being recognized. The IP had to re-establish both the position and the planned track.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of awareness of position after an unplanned deviation around cloud, was unable to state the aircraft position relative to the planned track when asked. Orientation was regained only with the IP pointing out the ground features. By that time the track error was at the 2 NM limit.
texts.2: SP, due to a chart-to-ground comparison interrupted during the turn onto the new leg, was briefly uncertain of position after roll-out. SP used the next major ground feature to re-establish orientation, identified a one to two mile track error and corrected back toward the course line unaided.
texts.3: SP remained oriented throughout the route and was able to state the aircraft position relative to the planned track at any time. Chart features were matched to the ground continuously and the track was held within one mile.
texts.4: SP kept an accurate running position at all times and identified each ground feature before reaching it. Orientation was never in doubt, including after deviations around weather, and the planned track was regained immediately on each occasion.
texts.marginal: SP stayed oriented and inside the standards, but the position picture was rebuilt at each checkpoint rather than carried continuously between them. The trend is that an unplanned deviation would leave SP briefly uncertain of position. SP is expected to maintain a running position between checkpoints and be able to state it at any point on the leg.

texts_at.0: With the IP pointing out the ground feature needed to re-establish position, SP matched it to the chart and confirmed the aircraft location before continuing the leg. Carrying a running position between checkpoints, without needing a ground feature pointed out, has not yet been introduced, so orientation still depends on the IP's guidance at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin naming a ground feature independently after each unplanned deviation, with the IP still available to confirm it, before a running position is required unaided.
texts_at.1: SP re-established orientation with the track error at about 1.8 NM, using the next major ground feature after an unplanned deviation around cloud. Awareness of position lapsed briefly because the chart-to-ground comparison was not resumed immediately after the deviation ended. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to resume the chart-to-ground comparison as soon as a weather deviation ends, before a ground feature is needed to re-orient.
texts_at.2: SP re-established orientation with the track error at about 1.4 NM after a brief interruption in the chart-to-ground comparison during a turn. The uncertainty came from the comparison being interrupted right at the point where a new leg's picture needed to be built. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the chart-to-ground comparison before starting the turn onto a new leg rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP remained oriented throughout the route and held the track error to about 0.7 NM on the leg where a brief check was needed. The small uncertainty came from a ground feature that took a moment longer than usual to positively match to the chart. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to keep a second candidate feature in mind on legs with fewer distinctive landmarks so a match is available immediately.

texts_above.1: SP re-established orientation using the next major ground feature and closed the resulting track error to about 1.85 NM before the planned track was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP re-established a running position at about 1.3 NM of track error by using the next major ground feature immediately after an unplanned deviation, without needing to be prompted. Resuming the chart-to-ground comparison a few seconds earlier, right as the deviation ended, would close that gap sooner still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable orientation recovery.
texts_above.3: SP held the track error to about 0.7 NM by keeping the chart-to-ground comparison running continuously through the turns rather than only on the straight legs. The technique is already sound; only the busiest turning points still draw the comparison out for a moment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good running position awareness.
texts_above.4: SP kept an accurate running position at all times, holding the track error inside about 0.2 NM even through an unplanned deviation around weather. The only refinement available was to call the position out loud at each feature for the record, since the awareness itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior position awareness.

error_modes.label: Cockpit task sequencing around turning points

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the chart work, the log entries and the radio calls inside the turn onto the new leg, did not fly the aircraft accurately while those tasks were completed. The heading was allowed to wander, checkpoints were missed and the track error exceeded 2 NM. The IP intervened to fly the aircraft back onto the planned course line.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate workload management around the turning points, fell behind the route and completed the log and time entries well after each checkpoint. Aircraft handling degraded while the tasks were caught up and the track error reached the 2 NM limit. The correction was made only after the IP prompted a return to course.
texts.2: SP, due to cockpit tasks started at the checkpoint rather than before it, allowed a one to two mile track error to develop while the log was being completed. SP recognized the divergence, gave priority to flying the correction heading over the paperwork and regained the course line before the next checkpoint.
texts.3: SP sequenced the navigation tasks so that chart work and log entries were completed without degrading aircraft control. Checkpoints were identified on time and the track was held within one mile throughout the route.
texts.4: SP prepared each leg before reaching the turning point, so heading, time and fuel entries were made with the aircraft flown precisely. Workload stayed evenly distributed across the route and no cockpit task was allowed to compete with holding the planned track.
texts.marginal: SP completed the navigation tasks and held the track within the standards, but the workload was consistently bunched at the turning points. The trend is that any additional cockpit task at a turn would displace the track correction. SP is expected to prepare the next leg before the turning point so that the correction angle is set on roll-out.

texts_at.0: With the IP prompting the return to the course heading while SP completed the log and time entries, SP gave priority to the correction once it was called. Sequencing chart work, log entries and the radio call around the turning point, without the correction being prompted, has not yet been asked of SP, so task priority still comes from the IP's call at this stage. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin starting the log entry before reaching the checkpoint, with the IP still available to call the correction, before the sequencing is required unaided.
texts_at.1: SP completed the log and time entries with the track error at about 1.9 NM while catching up on tasks bunched at the turning point. The workload built up because the chart work, the log entries and the radio call were all started at the checkpoint rather than before it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to start the log entry before reaching the checkpoint so flying the correction is not left competing with paperwork.
texts_at.2: SP completed the cockpit tasks with the track error held to about 1.4 NM while giving priority to the correction heading over the log entry. The bunching came from starting the chart work at the checkpoint instead of on the approach to it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to begin the chart work while still inbound to the checkpoint so no task competes with the turn.
texts_at.3: SP sequenced the navigation tasks so the track error stayed at about 0.6 NM even on the leg with the heaviest workload at the turning point. The brief residual came from a log entry that ran a few seconds past the turn before it was finished. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to complete the log entry fully before starting the turn so nothing is left running into it.

texts_above.1: SP completed the log and time entries and closed the resulting track error to about 1.9 NM once priority was given to the correction heading. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP sequenced chart work, log entries and the radio call so that the track error at each turning point stayed at about 1.3 NM, with flying the correction always given priority over paperwork. Moving the chart work fully onto the straight leg, ahead of the checkpoint, would leave even less for the turn to absorb. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured task sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP completed chart work and log entries without degrading aircraft control, holding the track error to about 0.6 NM through every turning point of the route. The technique is already sound; only the tightest checkpoint spacing still asks for a slightly earlier start to the chart work. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise cockpit task sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP prepared every leg before reaching the turning point, holding the track error inside about 0.2 NM with no cockpit task ever competing with the track. The only refinement available was to note the exact preparation sequence for the debrief, since the workload distribution itself needed no adjustment. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate workload distribution.

error_modes.label: Standard Closing Angle computation and hold time
error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d(8)(j) STANDARD COURSE CORRECTIONS (SCA) AND WINGTIP REFERENCES

texts.0: SP, due to a course correction flown as an arbitrary turn toward the line instead of the Standard Closing Angle, never established a closing geometry with the planned course. The SCA of 17,5 degrees for 210 KGS and the hold time of one minute for every mile off course were not applied, so the aircraft paralleled the course line displaced by more than 2 NM. The IP had to establish the closing heading and time the correction.
texts.1: SP, due to a closing angle held for an arbitrary period instead of one minute for every mile off course, rolled out back on the leg heading while the aircraft was still displaced. The residual error stayed at the 2 NM limit until the IP called for the correction to be re-applied. The course line was regained only during the following leg.
texts.2: SP, due to an SCA started without a firm estimate of the miles off course, held the closing angle for too short a time and remained between 1 and 2 NM from the planned line. SP recognized the shortfall at the next ground reference, re-applied the 17,5 degree correction for the remaining distance and was back on the course line before the checkpoint. No prompting was required.
texts.3: SP applied the Standard Closing Angle derived from the 60-1 rule and held it for one minute for every mile off course. The aircraft closed the planned line without overshoot and track error stayed inside 1 NM for the remainder of the leg.
texts.4: SP computed the SCA for the actual ground speed, applied it as soon as the offset was detected and stopped the correction exactly on the course line. Residual displacement was not measurable on the chart and no second correction was needed.
texts.marginal: SP used the Standard Closing Angle and stayed inside the standards, but the hold time was judged by eye rather than counted as one minute for every mile off course. The trend is a correction that stops slightly short and leaves a small residual offset on each leg. SP is expected to time the SCA against the estimated miles off course and to stop it on the course line.

texts_at.0: With the IP computing the Standard Closing Angle and calling the hold time of one minute for every mile off course, SP flew the heading given and rolled out when the IP called the course line reached. Computing the SCA from the 60-1 rule and timing the hold independently have not yet been introduced, so the closing geometry still comes from the IP's call at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin estimating the miles off course out loud, with the IP still computing the SCA and the hold time, before an independent correction is required.
texts_at.1: SP re-applied the Standard Closing Angle with the residual displacement at about 1.9 NM before the course line was regained on the following leg. The shortfall came from holding the closing angle for a period judged by eye instead of the one minute for every mile off course. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to time the SCA against the estimated miles off course rather than judging the hold time visually.
texts_at.2: SP re-applied the 17,5 degree correction with the displacement held to about 1.4 NM before closing back to the course line. The shortfall came from starting the SCA without a firm estimate of the miles actually off course. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to estimate the miles off course before starting the SCA so the hold time is set correctly the first time.
texts_at.3: SP applied the Standard Closing Angle from the 60-1 rule and held the track error to about 0.6 NM for the remainder of the leg. The small residual came from a hold time that ran a few seconds past the estimated correction. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to stop timing the SCA the instant the estimated miles off course have been accounted for.

texts_above.1: SP applied the Standard Closing Angle called by the IP and closed the displacement from the planned course line to about 1.9 NM before the hold time expired. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP applied the Standard Closing Angle and held it for close to one minute per mile off course, closing the track error to about 1.3 NM without overshoot. Estimating the miles off course a little earlier, before the SCA is started, would tighten the hold time further still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent SCA computation.

This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless Standard Closing Angle technique.

error_modes.label: Quantifying distance off course with wingtip references

With no wingtip reference or any other measure, the correction bore no relation to the actual error and displacement passed 2 NM. The IP had to state the position error and direct the correction.

The undersized correction left the aircraft at the 2 NM limit until the IP passed the correct distance off course.

texts.3: SP estimated the distance off course in half mile increments using the wingtip reference for the altitude flown. The correction was sized to that estimate and the aircraft was held inside 1 NM of the planned course line.
texts.4: SP quantified every offset in half mile increments and cross-checked the wingtip reference against ground features of known distance. Corrections matched the measured error, so track deviation stayed negligible for the whole route.
texts.marginal: SP kept track error inside the standards, but the distance off course was estimated only once the offset had become obvious rather than at each major checkpoint. The trend is a correction sized after the error has grown, which costs track accuracy on short legs. texts_at.0: With the IP reading the wingtip reference for the altitude flown and stating the distance off course in half mile increments, SP sized the correction to the figure given. error_modes.source: technique:8.19.6.d(8)(i) WEATHER DEVIATIONS (Deliberate Course Duration Method)

texts.3: SP circumnavigated the weather with the deliberate course duration method, turning a determined number of degrees off course, timing the outbound leg and returning with twice the original heading change for the same time. The route was rejoined inside 1 NM of the planned ground track.
texts.4: SP selected a deviation angle matched to the size of the weather, recorded the heading change and the times on the kneeboard and flew equal outbound and inbound legs. The aircraft rejoined the planned course line with no measurable offset and the updated ETA for the next checkpoints was ready on rejoin.
texts.marginal: SP rejoined the route inside the standards after the weather deviation, but the heading change and the deviation times were held in memory rather than recorded on the kneeboard. The trend is a rejoin whose accuracy depends on recall under a high cockpit workload. SP is expected to note the heading change and the times and to fly the inbound leg for the same duration as the outbound leg.

texts_at.0: With the IP selecting the deviation angle and calling the outbound time and the heading change to record, SP flew the heading given and turned back onto the inbound leg when the IP called the time. Selecting a deviation angle matched to the weather, and timing the deliberate course duration independently, have not yet been introduced, so the rejoin still depends on the IP's call at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin recording the heading change and the outbound time as they happen, with the IP still selecting the deviation angle, before an independent rejoin is required.
texts_at.1: SP rejoined the route with the displacement at about 1.9 NM after a deviation angle well above the recommended maximum of 70 degrees made the timed return unreliable. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the deviation angle at or below the recommended maximum of 70 degrees so the timed return stays reliable.
texts_at.2: SP compared the ground picture with the chart after the rejoin and closed the residual offset to about 1.4 NM, having noted the outbound time only after the turn away from the route had already begun. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to note the outbound time at the instant the turn away begins, not after it, so the inbound leg can be timed accurately from the start.
texts_at.3: SP circumnavigated the weather with the deliberate course duration method, timing the outbound leg and returning with twice the original heading change, and rejoined the route within about 0.6 NM of the planned track. The small residual came from an inbound leg flown a few seconds short of the full outbound time. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to time the inbound leg for the exact duration of the outbound leg, not a few seconds short of it.

texts_above.1: SP flew the deviation angle called by the IP and closed the resulting displacement from the planned course line to about 1.9 NM on rejoining the route. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP circumnavigated the weather using the deliberate course duration method, timing the outbound leg and doubling the heading change for the return, and rejoined the route within about 1.3 NM of the planned track. Recording the outbound time and the heading change on the kneeboard as they happened, rather than from memory, would tighten the rejoin further still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent weather circumnavigation technique.
texts_above.3: SP selected a deviation angle matched to the weather, recorded the heading change and the times on the kneeboard, and rejoined the planned course line within about 0.6 NM after flying equal outbound and inbound legs. The technique is already sound; only an unusually irregular weather cell still asks for the deviation angle to be reassessed partway through. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined course duration technique.
texts_above.4: SP selected a deviation angle matched to the size of the weather and flew equal outbound and inbound legs, rejoining the planned course line inside about 0.2 NM with the updated ETA ready at the moment of rejoin. The only refinement available was to note the exact deviation angle used for the debrief, since the rejoin itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless weather circumnavigation technique.
